chunks: Al-Saffar from Muhammad ibn 'Isa ibn 'Ubayd from 'Ali ibn Sulayman said:

I said: A man comes to me and says to me, 'Buy for me a garment for a dinar, or less, or more.' So I buy it for him at the price he specifies. Then I tell him, 'This garment is for so-and-so, and so-and-so, for more than what I bought it for,' while I do not inform him that I have made a profit on it. And I have stipulated with its owner that he must pay the price I want, otherwise I will return it to him. Is the stipulation and the profit permissible, or is it pleasing to me to take something from it? And is it pleasing to me to make a profit on him if I was obligated to take it from the owner? He wrote: 'It is not pleasing to you to take anything from this, so do not do it.'

key_terms.اِسْتَوْجَبْتُهُ: I was obligated to take/secure it

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible for an agent to buy goods for a client and sell them at a higher price without disclosing the profit?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Al-Saffar reports that the Imam ruled against the validity of the secret profit in this specific agency model, stating 'nothing is pleasing to you from this,' which Shia jurists interpret as a prohibition (or strong disapproval) of keeping the surplus when the agent was bound to a specific price. This highlights the Shia emphasis on *adl* (justice) and transparency in *wakalah*, distinguishing between a fixed fee and hidden markup. The ruling underscores that the agent's obligation to the principal requires clear accounting of the purchase price to avoid *gharar* (uncertainty) or unjust enrichment.
